content.title: Denny Hamlin finds support in return to Phoenix, where agonizing offseason began
content.text: AVONDALE, Ariz. — A young boy, likely no older than 7, approached the autograph table with a future Hall of Fame NASCAR driver behind it and asked for a photo.“Can we do the double ‘ones?'” the boy asked, holding up a bent knuckle on each hand.Denny Hamlin has heard such requests before; after all, he’s driven the No. 11 car for the past 20 years. So he held out a pair of index fingers — double ‘ones’ — to form an 11 and smiled for the picture.“No,” the boy’s mother corrected. “Ones, like middle fingers.”Hamlin was taken aback. Getting flipped off is a gesture he’s seen hundreds of times during his career as one of NASCAR’s great antagonists, the result of a fan base that spent a generation disliking his brashness and struggling to relate to his personality and lifestyle.Your browser does not support the video tag.But here, at an autograph session 30 minutes from Phoenix Raceway, there was no animosity to be found. Hamlin has come full circle with NASCAR fans, who now regularly cheer him during the pre-race driver introductions each week instead of showering him with boos.Hamlin politely declined the boy’s offer to hold up the middle fingers himself and stuck with the more, uh, traditional way to express a No. 11 with one’s hands. But the boy flashed the double birds as his delighted mother snapped a photo on her cell phone.“I saw him holding his knuckles like that, and I thought, ‘Surely, he’s not … !'” Hamlin said, laughing. “Wow!”It’s good for Hamlin to laugh these days, particularly during a return to Phoenix. Of all places, last weekend figured to trigger some painful memories that remain all too fresh.Just four months ago, during NASCAR’s last visit here, Hamlin suffered the most heartbreaking moment of his career. While dominating NASCAR’s championship race with just four laps to go, another car’s flat tire caused a caution and reset the field.Hamlin, the best driver never to win a NASCAR championship, lost the lead during the ensuing pit stops and could not recover before the checkered flag waved.As Kyle Larson celebrated the championship that day instead of him, Hamlin parked his car on pit road, took off his helmet and stared through the windshield into nothingness for what seemed like an eternity. Afterward, he floated the idea of immediate retirement, unsure if his heart was still in it enough to muster the required commitment it takes to be great in the NASCAR Cup Series.Hamlin and 23XI co-owner Michael Jordan’s lawsuit against NASCAR resulted in a ground-breaking settlement.Grant Baldwin / Getty ImagesThen came the offseason, which made the Phoenix heartbreak seem like a distant memory.First, Hamlin and 23XI Racing co-owner Michael Jordan sued NASCAR in a federal antitrust trial, a high-stakes gamble that threatened to either put their race team out of business or change the face of NASCAR. They successfully reached a settlement in mid-December that gave all teams a permanent franchise-like status for the first time in NASCAR’s nearly 80-year history, and Hamlin was on a high.But two weeks later, tragedy struck. On Dec. 28, his parents’ 52nd wedding anniversary, their house caught fire and burned to the ground. His father, Dennis, and mother, Mary Lou, were found outside the house when firefighters arrived. Dennis, who had been suffering from advanced COPD, died as a result of his injuries, and Mary Lou was hospitalized with severe injuries of her own.Hamlin, 45, ultimately decided to race again this season; next year is set to be the final year of his career. But while combing through the rubble of his parents’ home in January, he fell and aggravated a shoulder injury that needs surgery to repair — except doing so would cause him to miss much of this season.So he’s decided to put it off until the end of the year, racing through the physical pain while still dealing with the mental variety.But the NASCAR schedule never relents, and Hamlin was suddenly back to Phoenix for the first time since that fateful November weekend. Reminders of what happened then, and since, were never far away — even in the autograph line of his supporters at a Bob’s Discount Furniture store.“I’m so sorry about your offseason,” a man said as Hamlin signed his “DHXI” license plate. “So, so sorry.”“Thank you,” Hamlin said sincerely, looking up while scribbling his signature.Hamlin signs autographs at Bob’s Discount Furniture. His pursuit of an elusive title amid a tumultuous and tragic season endeared him to many fans.Jeff Gluck / The AthleticIn public-facing situations like these, the driver is never sure what he’s going to get. Though he spent the majority of his career in a villain role, clashing with more popular drivers and getting criticized for strong opinions on a number of topics, fans began to change their tune last summer.Hamlin showed emotion during a quest for career win No. 60 — good for 10th on NASCAR’s all-time wins list — because of his dad’s faltering health. And as he neared the long-awaited first championship, fans seemed to be ready to embrace him after a couple of decades of pushing him away.When it didn’t happen in Phoenix, many were crushed. When he stood up to NASCAR in the lawsuit, they took his side. When his parents had the house fire, they felt the loss.So now, as his career winds down, Hamlin is suddenly more popular than ever. And a mix of his new and longtime fans lined up at the Bob’s location to meet him, armed with all sorts of items and thoughts to share.One man showed Hamlin his No. 11 tattoo. Another told Hamlin their child was named after him. He signed old pieces of his car, a purple shoe belonging to a woman in socks (who promptly put the shoe back on) and a Labubu from a young girl, who clasped her hands together and held them to her mouth in an expression of joy as she watched his signature go on the toy.A woman approached Hamlin and presented him with a photo of her pet bird.“Everyone says his personality is just like yours,” she said.“I have a bird just like this!” Hamlin replied, then discussed details related to pet bird lingo that were unintelligible to a non-bird-owning sportswriter.One man walked up to the table with a baby’s onesie for Hamlin to sign.“I’ve been with you since Day 1,” he said, “and now my son will be here any day now.”Hamlin said he has a hard time wrapping his head around the sort of impact he has on people. As a Bill Elliott fan growing up, he recalls the access he had to his favorite driver came through watching Cup races on a Sunday afternoon and getting the occasional fan club letter in the mail.Now in the age of social media and podcasting (Hamlin’s “Actions Detrimental” is one of the most popular NASCAR podcasts), fans are in tune with what he’s doing on a near-daily basis.“I find it shocking I can be part of someone’s life as much as I am,” he said. “When you see these fans who have gear from the last 20 years, it’s like, ‘Oh wow, I mean a lot to them.’ And that reminds me what we do is pretty big.”As for the newer fans for a driver near retirement? Many of Hamlin’s former detractors have softened on him, he theorized, because of his father’s illness last year.“People just related it to their own lives,” he said. “They remember how it felt when their parents passed or when their brother got sick. And once they can relate to you, that’s when they start to be OK with you, because you’re not just this character they see on TV.”But that was a problem for much of Hamlin’s career. He wasn’t like other NASCAR drivers, who presented themselves with more of a down-home image.Hamlin has lived like a rock star with a mansion and a helipad and an indoor basketball court and bowling alley in his house. Little effort was made to relate to the common, blue-collar fan — even though he did not come from money, once working as a Subway sandwich artist and later in his father’s trailer-hitch shop.He still isn’t convinced this newfound positivity toward him will last. As is typical for someone in their mid-40s, Hamlin understands his faults and limitations — his unapologetic competitiveness and outspokenness among them.“There will be a time this year when the fans get over their emotions and connections for me, because I’ll do something that upsets them and they’re going to say, ‘That’s why I hated his ass,'” he said. “And I get it. I know I’m not for everyone.“When I play pickleball, I’m not even for my fiancée (Jordan Fish) because I talk s— and it hurts her feelings. I’m like, ‘This is part of the game! Toughen up.'”Bob’s Discount Furniture is one of Hamlin’s newest sponsors, and COO Ramesh Murthy, who was standing nearby, wasn’t around to see any of the negatives that used to make Hamlin one of the most-booed drivers.“He’s a strong competitor and a good guy,” Murthy said. “You watch him with all the folks here. He treats his fans like we like to treat our guests.”Suddenly, there’s a new guest at the autograph session, a woman who quietly enters the right side of Hamlin’s peripheral vision. It’s Mary Lou, his mother.Hamlin didn’t know she was coming, and had just been talking about her before the autograph session began. It seems Mary Lou had chosen what her son deemed to be a cringeworthy couch for her new home, but Hamlin was reluctant to push back too much.“Whatever you want, Mom. Whatever makes you happy,” he had told her.Hamlin looks on as his mom upgrades her couch.Jeff Gluck / The AthleticHamlin had been relaying that story to a reporter as he walked past the couches in the store, and of course, the Bob’s Discount Furniture people were all over that. So when Mary Lou unexpectedly showed up, she ended up couch shopping for a more agreeable piece of furniture for both mother and son.When all 150 people in the autograph line had their chance to meet Hamlin, he checked back with Mary Lou before exiting the store. It turned out she had selected an expansive couch called the “Slider Bob Power Sectional,” listed at $2,799, and Hamlin smiled.“This is way, way better,” he said.With that, Hamlin was out the door and back in the rental car to return to the racetrack. He had hours of studying ahead of him in hopes of getting his car good enough to get “a little redemption” from November, but he was skeptical there’d be enough speed to do so.As it turned out, he was right. His car wasn’t quite up to the task, and he finished fifth. There was no magical comeback on this day.It landed better, though. When Hamlin pulled his car back onto pit road at the end of the race, stopping mere feet from the spot where he processed his November heartbreak, he didn’t linger in the cockpit. He quickly undid his seatbelts, climbed out of the car and began debriefing with his team.Despite all the emotional ups and downs of the last four months, he was still competitive. He still had something left in the tank.“It’s easy to look in the moment and the weekend as ‘This is a success or failure,'” he said. “But this is a marathon. We’re just an inch into a mile. There’s a long way to go, but we’ve got something to build with.”
